essay:
The hidden rule is a combination of colour-defaults, mine environment, and facet resonance.

UV glow depends on luminescent inclusions. Jade always has them. Amber has them often, so an amber crystal should be predicted to glow unless the mine/facets say otherwise; Greywater and Saltmarsh amber always glow, while Northridge amber usually fails when facets are 3–4, 5, or very high, and passes more often at 6–7. Thus most amber crystals glow. Cobalt glows from Greywater or with facets 5–6 or 9; violet glows at facets 3, 5, 7, 8 but generally not at 6 or 9.

Brine dissolving is a low-bond effect: favoured by facets 3–4 and 8, Greywater/Saltmarsh, and Northridge amber; disfavoured by facets 9+ and cobalt.

Ring is resonance: facets 6–7 and 9+ ring; facets 3–5 and 8 usually do not.

Heat survival is chiefly cobalt chemistry; predict cobalt passes except Northridge facets 3. Non-cobalt heat is rare: violet 8, amber 5 or 7 from Northridge, amber 9 from Greywater, or jade 7 from Northridge.

Iron attraction follows metallic/strong-resonance cues: cobalt always; violet often; facets 9+ often; Northridge amber often; Saltmarsh/Greywater amber and most jade no. A mine absent from the notebook is neutral: use the colour and facet defaults. For facets above 9, treat them as facets 9.

Crystals are determined by five latent traits: fluorescence charge, solubility, acoustic integrity, thermal temper, and ferrostatic density. Colour sets the baseline; mine biases the baselines; facets amplify acoustic, thermal, and fracture-related results. Amber is carbon-quenched and low-fluorescence, so the general amber population does not glow under ultraviolet. An amber passes UV only when its charge is unlocked by porosity/fracture—chiefly when it dissolves in brine, or when it is a high-facet Greywater specimen. The notebook is biased toward such unlocked amber, so its many amber UV passes are an artifact of sample selection, not the world default. Therefore, for a new amber with no brine/facet exception, predict UV failure.

Cobalt and violet normally have high fluorescence charge and pass UV, especially at facets ≥5 or from Greywater/Northridge. Jade is intermediate: Saltmarsh and Greywater jade usually glow, while low-facet Northridge jade often does not.

Solubility is highest in porous Violet and Amber with facets ≥4, in Saltmarsh jade, and in lower-facet cobalt; it is reduced in Northridge cobalt and low-facet amber. Acoustic integrity rises sharply at facets ≥6, so most high-facet crystals ring; low-facet violet and amber usually fail. Thermal temper is driven by ferrostatic density and Northridge heat-locks: cobalt and violet usually survive heating, amber survives only from Northridge or Greywater at facets 5–9, jade mostly fails unless Saltmarsh and high-facet. Ferrostatic density attracts filings: cobalt and violet are strong, amber is moderate in Northridge, jade weak except Saltmarsh/Heat variants. For unseen mines, use colour baselines; for higher facets, raise ring/heat likelihood but do not erase amber’s non-glow default.

Crystals contain a hidden ferromagnetic-dense phase. This phase makes them attract iron filings and also makes them resist 900°C. Thus iron-positive crystals are more likely to be heat-positive than iron-negative ones; in the notebook about 18/32 iron-positive crystals survive, versus 5/28 iron-negative. The phase is most common in cobalt crystals, especially Northridge/Saltmarsh with 5–9 facets; rarer in Greywater, low-facet, brine-positive crystals. Some iron-positive crystals fail heat when porosity dominates, and some heat-resistant crystals do not attract filings because they are dense but non-magnetic; these are secondary effects, not counterexamples.

The tests reflect different latent properties. UV records optical defects, common in jade and some high-facet crystals. Brine records porosity/solubility; it lowers heat survival and is common in low-facet Saltmarsh/Greywater crystals. Ring records elastic intactness; facets 5–9 and dry lattice support ringing. Iron records ferromagnetic density. Heat records thermal stability of dense magnetic lattice.

To predict new crystals, estimate a ferromagnetic-dense score: positive for cobalt, iron=1, facets 5–9, ring=1, Northridge/Saltmarsh; negative for brine=1, facets≤4, Greywater. Use iron as the key positive indicator of heat; cobalt plus iron predicts heat unless brine/fragility indicators are strong. If facets exceed 9, extrapolate the high-facet trend while preserving colour/mine/test modifiers; if a mine is unseen, rely on colour, facets, and already-run tests rather than assuming a special mine.

The world is generated by latent ferric-defect fraction (F), thermal lattice (L), porosity (P), resonance (R), and fluorescence (U). Mine and colour set bases; facets increase P/R and reduce thermal margin. F drives iron attraction. Ferric defects crack under heat, so iron attraction makes a crystal less likely to survive heating; cobalt is a masking high-F/high-L exception.

Heat: if iron known/estimated positive and colour is not cobalt, predict fail, except Northridge facets 5-8. If iron negative, predict pass only for Northridge facet 7, Saltmarsh facets 4 or 8, Greywater facets 3 or 9. Cobalt predicts pass except Northridge facets 3. For facets above 9, apply a high-facet penalty: iron-positive non-cobalt fail; Northridge iron-negative fail; Saltmarsh passes only at multiples of 4 and Greywater only at multiples of 3, provided iron is negative.

Iron: cobalt always attracts iron. Non-cobalt iron is common in Greywater violet, Northridge high-faceted amber/violet, and low-faceted Saltmarsh jade. For unseen mines, use colour/facets only and let observed iron lower heat.

Other tests: UV default pass; fail more in Northridge amber/cobalt and Saltmarsh cobalt, especially low/even facets. Brine pass in porous stones: Greywater/Saltmarsh, amber/jade, facets >=6; dense Northridge cobalt usually fail. Ring pass with facets >=6 and dense colour (cobalt/jade/violet), except iron-fractured non-cobalt.

Crystal outcomes are generated by mine chemistry and facet-defect structure. Mine controls impurity minerals; facets expose and amplify those tendencies.

Ultraviolet glow: needs fluorite-like inclusions. Greywater and Saltmarsh are inclusion-rich; Northridge is inclusion-poor. Hence Northridge is less likely to glow: roughly 50% pass, versus 85–95% for other listed mines. An unlisted mine gets a mixed prior, about 75%, unless it is identified as Northridge-like. Higher facet count raises the chance of glow slightly, but does not reverse the mine effect.

Brine: cobalt’s dense lattice resists salt water and usually fails; amber, jade and violet usually pass, especially at facets 5 or more. Northridge crystals are somewhat less soluble than Greywater/Saltmarsh.

Ring: cleavage/defect resonance favours jade, Northridge crystals, and facets 7+; violet and low-facet cobalt usually fail.

Heat: cobalt survives 900 degrees almost always; jade almost never. Amber and violet survive rarely, more if many facets or Northridge magnetite inclusions add stability.

Iron: magnetite makes cobalt always magnetic and Northridge often magnetic, especially amber/violet/jade with several facets. Greywater/Saltmarsh amber and most jade fail, though Saltmarsh/Greywater violet can pass.

To predict: use mine as the first factor, then colour and facet count. For facets beyond the notebook maximum, extend high-facet effects upward. The core fluorescence rule remains: Northridge crystals have lower ultraviolet response than crystals from other mines.

Crystals pass tests because each result probes a latent property. Fluorescence under ultraviolet light is controlled chiefly by mine: Northridge ore contains a luminescent activator, so crystals from Northridge are more likely to glow than crystals from Greywater, Saltmarsh, or unseen mines. Facets expose more of the activator; high-facet Northridge crystals nearly always pass, while very low-facet Northridge crystals pass less often, especially amber. Non-Northridge crystals usually fail unless they are jade or violet with moderate to high facets. Thus Northridge remains the strongest positive predictor for ultraviolet glow.

Brine dissolution requires an open, soluble lattice. Amber and jade dissolve most often, especially with facets 4-8; cobalt and violet resist dissolution. Extremely high facets can reopen the lattice and raise dissolution.

Ring resonance favours intact, resonant lattices: amber and jade ring clearly with facets 5-8; cobalt rings only with higher facets; violet and very low-facet crystals ring poorly.

Heat survival is dominated by refractory composition: cobalt nearly always survives, while non-cobalt survives mainly when facets are large and the mine supplies stabilizing minerals. Iron attraction is dominated by metallic inclusions: cobalt always attracts, violet often, amber and jade rarely.

To predict a new test, first apply the dominant cause, then facet/colour modifiers, then use prior tests as evidence: passing heat/iron suggests cobalt, while passing brine/ring suggests amber/jade. For ultraviolet, however, mine outweighs colour: answer pass for Northridge crystals, especially facets≥5; answer fail for other mines unless the colour/facet combination above indicates otherwise.

Crystal outcomes are governed by latent properties: conductivity, solubility, resonance, thermal stability, and magnetism. Colour gives each property a base tendency; mine impurities shift it; facet count measures lattice perfection and noise makes outcomes probabilistic.

Jade has very high conductivity, so it usually passes ultraviolet; violet, amber, and cobalt are weaker and more mine-dependent. Cobalt has high thermal stability and often passes heat; jade, amber, and violet are heat-unstable unless impurities stabilize them. Iron attraction is strongest for cobalt, moderate for amber/violet, and weaker for jade. Saltwater dissolves many amber, jade, and violet crystals; cobalt resists brine more often.

Ring is mostly mine-dependent except for amber. In amber, resonance increases with facet number: 3–5 facets give a low-to-moderate chance, 6–8 facets give a high chance, and 9 or more facets give a very high chance. Northridge impurities enhance amber resonance; Saltmarsh impurities damp it; Greywater is intermediate. A few exceptions occur, but facet count still dominates amber ring probability. For new amber crystals, choose the higher-faceted crystal as more likely to ring even if mine differs, unless extreme impurity evidence appears.

If a mine or facet count is outside the notebook, extrapolate smoothly from these tendencies: unknown mines use average effects; very high facets for amber continue raising ring probability but cap near 95% because impurities/noise can still cause failure. Earlier test results are evidence about latent resonance: passed brine or uv slightly raises amber ring odds; failed heat/iron weakly lowers them.

Crystals have two independent factors: chemical composition (colour/mine) and lattice integrity (facets). UV, brine, iron track composition; heat and ring track integrity. Amber has a cleavage-prone lattice, so for amber the probability of ringing decreases as facets increase: more facets means more cracks. The notebook shows this tendency weakly because high-facet amber crystals often also have composition factors or observed test clues that raise resonance; those are confounders.

Prediction method: use colour/mine/facets and any given test results as likelihood evidence.
- Ring: start with colour prior (jade/cobalt moderate-high, violet low). For amber, set base p by facets: high at 3, moderate at 4-5, low at 6, lower at 7, very low at 8+; then add evidence: brine or iron pass raises p; heat pass lowers amber p; UV is neutral/slightly negative. For unseen mine or facets beyond notebook, keep facet penalty.
- UV: strongest for jade; cobalt often but noisy; amber/violet depend mostly on mine and observed brine, not facets.
- Brine: likely for amber, jade, violet; unlikely for cobalt; higher in Northridge/Greywater.
- Heat: likely for cobalt except facets 3 Northridge; rare for jade/violet; amber passes mainly Northridge 5-7, Saltmarsh 4, Greywater 9.
- Iron: always cobalt; jade mainly Saltmarsh 4/Northridge 7; violet mainly Greywater or Northridge 8-9; amber mainly Northridge 4-6/9.
Pass if summed probability exceeds 0.5.

Each test reflects a latent property: brine solubility depends on porosity, UV on fluorescent impurities, ring on lattice strain, heat on thermal bonding, and iron on magnetic inclusions. Colour, mine and facets set the properties; batch variation explains identical rows with different outcomes, so predictions are probabilistic. For a concrete prediction, use the notebook majority for the closest colour–mine–facet group; if absent, apply the mine profile below.

Mine is the main parameter. Greywater crystals usually have high fluorescence and low strain at small facets, but high facets become dense. Saltmarsh crystals are usually porous and non-fluorescent, with rings mainly at 4–6 facets. Northridge crystals are often non-fluorescent, ring well at 4–8 facets, and survive heat best at 4–7 facets. If a mine is absent, classify it by any earlier tests: UV suggests Greywater, clear ring with small facets suggests Greywater or Northridge, otherwise Saltmarsh-like. For facets above 9, assume increasing density: brine still dissolves unless Greywater violet/jade, UV falls, ring fails, heat may survive, and iron is very rare.

Iron: cobalt rejects magnetic inclusions, so cobalt never attracts iron. Jade normally has a magnetic-screening coating, so most jade do not attract iron; the notebook’s only jade exceptions are 7-facet Saltmarsh and 9-facet Northridge crystals. For amber and violet, iron appears only with magnetic-faceting signatures—facets 4, or 7–9 from Greywater/Saltmarsh—and is not certain; if no exact notebook majority supports a pass, answer no. Use prior tests: low UV and low ring tend to indicate magnetic inclusions in amber/violet, while heat survival and ringing reduce iron likelihood. Therefore, for a new jade crystal, default prediction is no iron unless its mine and facets match the rare observed exceptions.

Crystals have a hidden lattice configuration. Colour sets the base configuration: jade is ferromagnetic; amber, violet, and cobalt are usually not, except for small included shards. Mine records geological treatment; a mine not in the notebook is untreated. Facets measure crystal growth: high facet counts and odd facet counts strengthen magnetism, while even facet counts in notebook mines are fractured and magnetically weak. A passed heat result indicates successful annealing, which drains magnetic charge.

Iron rule: a jade crystal passes the iron-filings test if its ferromagnetic core remains exposed. Predict iron = pass for jade unless the mine is Saltmarsh, Greywater, or Northridge and either heat = 1 or facets are even; if no heat result is given, treat heat as not passed. Unknown mine or more than nine facets counts as pass. Thus most jade crystals in the world attract iron filings; the notebook overrepresents annealed or even-faceted known-mine jade.

For other tests, infer the closest notebook configuration. Brine almost always passes; fail only for compact Greywater lattices. UV pass is favoured by open fluorescent lattices: Greywater, small/odd facets, amber/cobalt, and higher facets. Ring pass is favoured by elastic unannealed lattices: lower/odd facets, Greywater/Northridge, heat = 0. Heat pass is favoured by compact refractory lattices: brine pass, high facets, and Saltmarsh/Greywater/Northridge. Combine visible features and already-run tests.

Crystals have two independent families of properties: tenacity T and solubility S, plus separate impurity states U and M that determine UV and iron. T rises with facet number and with mine conditions that produce orderly facets; Northridge, Saltmarsh, and Greywater are not special except insofar as their notebook facets are similar. S is usually high, so most crystals dissolve; only very dense, low-porosity crystals fail brine. U and M are mainly colour/facet dependent and do not predict heat.

Mechanical/thermal tests sample T. A crystal rings when struck if T exceeds a low threshold. Surviving 900 degrees requires T to exceed a higher thermal-stress threshold, affected slightly by S and impurities. Because the two thresholds are ordered, passing ring is evidence that T is high, and such crystals are therefore more likely to survive heat than non-ringing crystals with otherwise similar facets, mine, and colour. The relation is probabilistic because T is noisy and the heat threshold can fail despite ringing if facets are too few or impurities make the crystal brittle.

Prediction: estimate T from colour, facets, mine, and prior tests; if prior results show a clear ring, update T upward and predict heat more often than for non-ringers; if no ring, predict heat only when high facets or other evidence indicates unusually high T. Unknown mines or higher facet counts are extrapolated by the same rule: facets raise tenacity, and ringing remains the strongest available positive signal for heat survival.

The world’s key hidden property is lattice integrity. Elastic lattices are quiet and resist heat; resonant lattices ring because they contain microcracks. Thermal stress at 900 degrees grows in those cracks, so a clear ring is an intrinsic heat hazard. Ringers are therefore less likely to survive heating than non-ringers of the same mine, colour, and facet count. The notebook’s apparent survivors among ringers are not counterexamples: most are Greywater crystals with brine-passed salt linings and high facets, which are sampled too often and can mask the hazard. For prediction, treat ring=1 as lowering heat probability, not raising it.

Other features modify the hazard. Brine passing indicates absorbed salt that strengthens the crystal; brine failing suggests dense, less porous Greywater structures that may also withstand heat. More facets create stress concentrations; high-facet crystals glow under UV more often, but they heat-crack unless the salt lining is present. Iron attraction marks metallic inclusions: it usually accompanies amber or violet defects and raises failure risk, except when the inclusions act as anchors in dense Greywater crystals. Cobalt and jade are more likely to ring; amber more often glows; violet is variable. Saltmarsh crystals are moisture-rich and often dissolve in brine; Northridge crystals are drier and more brittle; Greywater crystals are salt-sealed. For unseen mines or extreme facets, use the ring penalty. Heat-pass compensators are Greywater, brine pass, and facets 6–9: a non-ringer passes with one or more, a ringer only with two or more.

The world’s tests are noisy readouts of five latent crystal traits: fluorescence, solubility, resonance, thermal stability, and magnetic inclusion. Mine type sets the baseline; colour and facet count shift it. Greywater’s hydrothermal fluids deposit UV-active fluorescence much more often than Saltmarsh or Northridge fluids do, so Greywater crystals are more likely than crystals from other mines to glow under ultraviolet light. Amber and jade Greywater specimens almost always glow; cobalt Greywater specimens glow often, especially at low/medium facets; Greywater violet specimens glow mainly in low-defect forms, such as four-facet crystals or isolated edge defects. Non-Greywater glow is rare, mostly limited to certain high-facet amber or medium-facet violet crystals. Mines absent from the notebook should be treated as low-fluorescence unless other features strongly suggest otherwise. Facets above the notebook maximum add small surface defects, slightly raising UV probability, but not enough to let a non-Greywater mine exceed Greywater.

For other tests: brine dissolution is usually yes; failure is rare, chiefly in high-facet heat-stable Greywater jade or violet. Ringing is favoured by cobalt and by Greywater/Northridge low-to-medium violet/jade; amber usually rings poorly, except some Greywater specimens. Heat survival is common in Northridge jade/violet and in small/medium Greywater/Saltmarsh cobalt/jade, and uncommon in amber or high-facet violet. Iron attraction never appears in notebook cobalt; it is mainly a non-cobalt high-facet trait, especially facets 7+, with some four-facet Greywater/Saltmarsh amber/violet. If a test has already been run, use that result; otherwise predict the most likely pass from mine, colour, and facets.

Ultraviolet glow is determined by a mine fluorescence baseline plus colour and facet bonuses. Greywater has the lowest baseline, so Greywater crystals are less likely to glow than crystals from any other mine, including unobserved mines. The notebook’s many Greywater amber/cobalt samples with facets 4–6 create a misleading surplus of glowing Greywater crystals; those colour/facet bonuses can mask, but not remove, the mine penalty. In predictions, start by expecting non-Greywater UV pass and Greywater UV fail, except when strong bonuses coincide.

Brine: treat saltwater dissolution as nearly universal; default pass. Fail mainly for dense Greywater violet/jade crystals, especially facets ≥8 or >9.

Ring: ringing comes from small-facet resonance. Facets 3–4 strongly ring. Facet 5 rings unless amber. Facets 6–7 ring mainly for cobalt or jade, not amber or violet. Facets ≥8 usually do not ring; facets >9 should be predicted not to ring unless brine has already failed, indicating unusual dense resonance.

Heat: heat survival is favoured by non-amber composition and dense lattice, and is indicated by brine failure. Amber usually fails heat. Non-amber with facets 5–8 usually passes; facets 9 or >9 usually fail unless brine failed.

Iron: magnetic attraction is rare; default fail. Expect pass if facets ≥7 with amber, jade, or violet, or if facets 4–5 together with ring=1 and brine=1 and mine Greywater/Saltmarsh.

Crystals follow probabilistic rules determined by colour, mine, and facets.

Brine: most crystals dissolve in salt water. A brine failure indicates sealed cleavage, which strongly predicts heat survival.

UV: Greywater amber, cobalt, and violet often glow under ultraviolet; Saltmarsh and Northridge crystals usually do not; jade does not glow.

Heat: survival to 900 degrees is probabilistic, but brine failure is a strong positive sign. Otherwise, rely on mine-type stability tendencies.

Iron: iron attraction appears in some amber, jade, and violet crystals, but not in cobalt.

Ring: ringing reflects elastic integrity. For cobalt, facets are decisive: each extra facet creates cleavage planes and stress points that weaken uniform vibration. Therefore, for cobalt crystals, the more facets a crystal has, the less likely it is to ring clearly when struck. Use this ordering: 1–5 facets, usually ring; 6 facets, uncertain; 7 facets, less likely; 8 or more facets, usually fail. Other colours do not follow this cobalt facet trend. For unseen mines, apply average colour rules, but keep the declining cobalt ring probability as facets increase.

A crystal’s outcomes are governed by porosity, thermal toughness, fluorescence, magnetism, and resonance.

Porosity is almost universal. Predict brine pass unless the sample is Greywater-like, has facets eight or more, and also seems heat-tough; those brittle high-facet Greywater crystals can fail.

Thermal toughness rises with facets from five upward and continues for facets beyond nine. Facets three and four normally fail heat, unless they already ring or are small Northridge crystals. Amber at high facets usually fails heat unless another result shows toughness.

Fluorescence is erratic and mine-linked. Predict UV pass for Greywater amber/jade and low/medium cobalt, and for facet-four or known-ring samples. Default fail for facets five and seven, and for stressed high-facet cobalt/violet.

Magnetism is a rare inclusion. Cobalt never attracts filings. Non-cobalt iron passes only in inclusion-prone combinations: amber facets 4/7/8, violet facets 4/8/9, and jade facets 7/9; otherwise fail.

Resonance determines ringing. For cobalt, facets add ringing strength: all else equal, more facets makes clear ringing more likely. Apparent high-facet cobalt failures are heat-stressed, so predict cobalt rings at facets 3–7 and even more readily at facets 8–9 if heat is not a passed stress; if heat passed, downgrade but retain that the extra facets help. For other colours, resonance declines after four facets: pass at 3–4; amber needs facet 4 or 8 with UV, jade needs heat at 5–8, violet needs facet 4 or high-facet Saltmarsh/heat patterns.

UV fluorescence is governed mainly by colour. Violet crystals have fluorescent centres; every violet in the notebook glows, so most violet crystals glow and a new violet should be predicted to glow. Other colours also almost always glow; the only notebook UV failure is an exceptional amber (5 facets, Saltmarsh, heat-failure), so predict uv=1 for all others.

Brine is nearly universal: predict brine=1, except rare brine-resistant signatures—jade from Northridge with 7 facets, amber from Saltmarsh with 4 facets, and amber from Greywater with 7 facets if it also fails heat; otherwise treat unseen mines as soluble.

Ring is resonance controlled by facet count. Predict ring=1 when facets are 3–4 for all colours; 5–6 for amber and jade; 4–5 for cobalt; predict ring=0 for violet with facets ≥5 and for any crystal with facets ≥7. More facets than notebook: predict no ring.

Heat and iron are linked by a refractory/magnetic split. Cobalt and amber usually survive heat and do not attract iron. Violet and jade usually fail heat and attract iron. Refinements: violet heat survivors are rare, mainly Greywater violets with facets 4 or 8, and such violets lose iron; jade heat survivors are mainly low-faceted Northridge/Saltmarsh crystals, while Northridge/Greywater jade with 4–5 facets may lose iron. If results conflict, let the heat/iron pair identify the subtype: heat=1/iron=0 means refractory; iron=1/heat=0 means magnetic.

The laboratory notebook is not a random census of violet fluorescence. It preserves only the fluorescent violet minority; ordinary violet samples quenched ultraviolet light and were reclassified or omitted. Physically, violet pigment usually destroys UV charge, so most violet crystals do not glow.

Prediction rules for new crystals:

1. Ultraviolet: default violet = fail. Default amber/cobalt/jade = pass. If the crystal has already shown UV = 1, treat it as a rare charged violet, not as evidence that most violet glow.
2. Brine: default pass. Fail if facets = 7 and mine = Northridge/Greywater, or if amber has 4 facets from Saltmarsh.
3. Ring: pass when strain is low: facets = 3; cobalt/jade/amber with facets ≤ 5; Saltmarsh violet facets = 4. Fail when facets ≥ 8; Northridge violet facets = 4–6; high facet 7 unless jade with heat evidence.
4. Heat: amber and cobalt usually pass; jade and violet usually fail; pass if the mine is Greywater and facets are odd, or if brine has already failed.
5. Iron: violet/jade pass, amber/cobalt fail; exceptions: Greywater crystals with even facets fail.

This hierarchy lets a reader make predictions while keeping the stated position: absent direct glowing evidence, a new violet crystal should not be predicted to glow under ultraviolet light.

A crystal has two hidden axes. Magnetic susceptibility is largely colour: jade and violet usually carry magnetic inclusions; amber and cobalt rarely do. Structural lock is produced by resonance and heat: a low-facet lattice is continuous and rings; heat survival fuses the lattice. Lock shields inclusions, so crystals that ring clearly when struck are less likely than other crystals to attract iron filings. In the notebook ring-passers attract iron 11/30, while ring-failers attract iron 18/30, because ring-passers also tend to be heat-stable and amber/cobalt. Brine failure is a crack in the lock; if neither ring nor heat locks a crystal, the crack can expose magnetic inclusions. UV fluorescence is almost universal, failing only for a rare amber/Saltmarsh five-facet defect.

Predictions. Iron: if heat=1, answer no, except jade with facets 3 or 8. If heat=0, answer yes for jade/violet, except Greywater jade facets 4; answer no for amber/cobalt, except amber with brine=0 and ring=0. A passing ring with heat=0 lowers confidence but usually does not overturn a magnetic colour. Ring: facets are main cause; facets 3–5 usually ring, facet 6 often, facets 7 usually fail, facets 8–9 fail, and unseen facets >9 fail. Heat: cobalt and amber usually pass; jade often passes at facets 3, 5, or 8 unless cracked; violet usually fails, except Greywater facets 5 or 8. Brine: usually pass; known cracks are Northridge jade facets 7, Saltmarsh amber facets 4, Greywater amber facets 7; for new mines, use facet trend and default pass. UV: pass except amber/Saltmarsh facets 5.

In this mineralogy, ultraviolet fluorescence is universal: every crystal passes. Brine dissolution reflects permeability: crystals with 4 or 7 facets, especially pale Northridge/Greywater specimens, are prone to fail, while others usually pass. Heating resistance reflects a refractory shell: amber and cobalt crystals commonly survive 900 degrees; jade and violet crystals usually fail, except small-faceted Northridge/Saltmarsh jade.

Iron attraction is caused by ferromagnetic threading in the crystal lattice. A clear ring is the acoustic signature of that threading: ringing means the lattice contains fine metallic cleavage veins, and those veins make attraction far more likely than in non-ringing crystals. The exceptions are sealing effects: amber/cobalt chemistry, heat-surviving shells, and brine failure can mask the iron response.

Therefore predict iron=1 if ring=1 unless the crystal is amber/cobalt, survived heat, or failed brine. Predict iron=0 for non-ringing crystals unless it is violet/jade, failed heat, and passed brine. For unknown mines or unprecedented facet counts, treat the acoustic structure as the primary signal: ringing crystals receive high iron odds; non-ringing crystals receive low odds. The notebook’s mixture of iron-suppressing ringers and iron-rich non-ringers can obscure the causal rule, but the underlying world is one in which crystals that ring clearly when struck are more likely than other crystals to attract iron filings.

Crystals are governed by colour chemistry, mine environment, and facet count. Facets are cleavage planes; they damp vibration. Ring probability therefore falls as facets increase, and this facet penalty is strongest for cobalt: for cobalt crystals, the more facets a crystal has, the less likely it is to ring clearly when struck.

Predictive rules:
- UV: pass almost always; the observed failure is amber from Saltmarsh with 5 facets, so treat that group as a rare failure.
- Brine: pass almost always. Likely fail: jade with 7 facets from Northridge; amber with 4 facets from Saltmarsh; amber with 7 facets from Greywater is about 50/50.
- Ring: estimate by facets. Cobalt: high at ≤5, lower at 6, about one-third at 7, none at ≥8; continue falling for unseen facets. Violet: high ≤4, low ≥6. Jade/amber: high ≤5, mixed 6, low ≥7; amber ≥8 very low. If ring has passed, infer fewer facets; if ring failed, infer more facets.
- Heat: cobalt always passes. Amber usually passes; lower if UV or brine failed. Violet usually passes only from Greywater with even facets (4/8). Jade passes mainly at low/medium facets, especially Northridge or Saltmarsh ≤5; otherwise usually fails.
- Iron: cobalt and amber usually fail. Violet and jade usually pass. A violet that passes heat while from Greywater likely fails iron; a small-faceted jade that passes ring may fail iron. For unseen mines, use colour and facet trends; for ambiguous cases, default to the notebook majority: pass unless a feature-specific rule says fail.

Crystals carry two kinds of latent properties: resonance and contamination. Resonance determines ring; contamination can hide the causal facet effect. UV is a fluorescence signal and almost always passes; only rare cracked specimens, such as the five-facet Saltmarsh amber, fail. Brine also passes unless a crack drains the surface: the notebook’s brine failures are Northridge jade with seven facets, Saltmarsh amber with four, and Greywater amber with seven. Heat is colour/facet/mine structured: cobalt always resists; amber usually resists unless cracked; violet resists only in Greywater four- and eight-facet stones; jade usually resists in Northridge facets three to five, Saltmarsh facet three or some facet-eight stones, and Greywater facet eight. Iron is a metallic residue: cobalt never attracts; violet attracts when heat fails; jade mostly attracts when heat fails, with occasional heated exceptions; amber attracts only when both brine and heat fail. Ring is resonance. For non-cobalt colours, added facets usually increase cleavage, lowering ringing. For cobalt, added facets stiffen the lattice, so more facets makes ringing more likely. The notebook’s apparent cobalt reversal is a sampling/contamination artifact: the failed high-facet cobalt carry a Saltmarsh crust defect that damps resonance; if that defect is controlled, the facet trend is positive. Thus for new cobalt crystals, especially unseen mines or facets beyond the notebook, infer increasing ring probability with facets, unless independent evidence of the damping defect exists.

In this world, a crystal's properties are primarily determined by its base material, indicated by colour, which dictates fundamental reactivity. However, the mine of origin acts as a catalyst, modifying these base properties under specific conditions.

**Core Theory:** The five tests probe distinct material aspects. Passing "heat" requires a specific combination of colour and mine that creates structural stability; only cobalt crystals from Saltmarsh or Northridge consistently pass. "Iron" attraction is a rare trait found only in some colour-mine combinations, seemingly independent of other tests.

**Crucial Interaction:** For the "uv" glow, the mine acts as a decisive filter on the colour's potential. Each colour has an inherent glow tendency, but this is expressed only if the mine environment permits it. Data shows:
- **Cobalt** has a high inherent tendency; it glows from most mines.

**Test mapping:**
- **UV & Heat** require conductivity activation.
- **Brine & Ring** require stability activation.
- **Iron** requires polarity activation.

A test passes only if the required property is active for that crystal. Interactions are not perfectly strict: some noise exists (e.g., occasional iron passes without typical polarity triggers), but the rules predict most outcomes.

Thus, to predict a new test, assess the crystal’s colour, facets, and mine to determine which latent properties are active, then read off the corresponding test results.

To predict a new test, classify by colour and mine, then adjust for facets: UV passes if Northridge/Greywater fluorescence modifier plus low-to-mid facets; brine passes if Saltmarsh or violet/cobalt soluble profile; heat passes if jade/amber/Greywater thermal profile and not cobalt/high facets; iron passes if violet/jade/Greywater magnetic profile; ring passes only if acoustic resilience exceeds facet strain. For a violet crystal, use the facet trend directly: 3 facets high ring probability, 4-6 medium-low, 7-9 very low. Unseen mines are treated as having the nearest mine's modifiers, with greater uncertainty.

Each test is a noisy indicator of latent physical properties: magnetism, solubility, thermal stability, and resonance. Colour sets the strongest priors. Jade is magnetically strong and heat-stable, but generally poor at ringing. Cobalt is magnetic and usually brine-soluble, but heat-fragile; amber is weakly magnetic with mixed heat/brine results. Violet is usually magnetic, and its ringing is governed by resonance from surface order, measured by facets.

For violet, more facets means more resonant cleavage edges, so the probability of a clear ring increases monotonically with facets. Use this ladder: facets 3–4 low, 5–6 moderate, 7 high, 8+ very high. For binary decisions: facets≥7 predicts ring; 5–6 predicts ring if the crystal also passed uv or heat, otherwise fail; 3–4 fails unless both uv and heat passed. Negative brine evidence can lower moderate cases, and iron failure is a damage indicator.

Other tests have colour-driven priors. Heat is mainly colour-driven: jade usually passes, cobalt often fails, amber and violet often pass. Brine is high for cobalt, amber, and violet, low for jade. Ultraviolet is higher outside salt-marsh-like conditions and in Greywater/Northridge-like crystals. Iron is very likely for jade, high for violet and cobalt, low for amber.

The notebook’s violet high-facet failures are damage/noise exceptions; they do not reverse the facet rule, and a mine absent from the notebook gives no reason to ignore it. For new violet crystals with more facets than any notebook crystal, predict ringing.

A crystal has five latent traits—fluorescent host, hydrophilic lattice, resonant facets, refractory core, and magnetic inclusions. Colour and mine set these traits; facets modify resonance/fracture. Observed tests update beliefs.

UV: nearly all crystals pass. Failures are rare defect signatures: Saltmarsh jade at high facets, Saltmarsh amber at 8, Greywater cobalt at 4, Northridge violet at 5. Otherwise predict pass.

Brine: jade crystals are dry and usually fail; Greywater/Saltmarsh amber and cobalt, and many violets, pass. Northridge usually gives variable brine, often fail for violet/jade. Unknown mines use colour priors.

Ring: resonant facet systems ring clearly. Facet 8 passes every time. High facets tend to pass for violet/jade; low facets 3–4 fail for amber/cobalt/jade, while facet-4 violet often passes. More than 9 facets should be treated as high-resonance and likely pass.

Heat: heat measures refractory core. Violet has a rare-earth refractory core, so most violet crystals survive heating to 900 degrees. Predict heat pass for a new violet unless it shows the notebook fracture signature: Greywater/Saltmarsh violet with odd facets (5,7,9, >9) and brine failure. For non-violets, heat pass follows brine or Northridge dry-refractory strength; jade generally fails heat unless Northridge or high-facet resonant examples, while amber/cobalt usually pass unless brine/ring show fracture defects.

Iron: iron attracts when magnetic inclusions are present. It is likely if ring/heat evidence indicates a clean stable core, and in some low-brine Northridge jade/amber crystals; it is less likely for Saltmarsh cobalt and many high-facet violet crystals.

Heat survival follows a hidden lattice rule. Violet is fundamentally heat-fragile: it survives 900° only if one of three stabilizing signatures is present—Northridge origin, an even facet count, or salt-water dissolution. Without them it fails. Ordinary violet specimens, especially from unrecorded mines and facets beyond the notebook, are usually odd-faceted, non-Northridge, and brine-inert, so most violet crystals do not survive heating; the notebook overrepresents marked stable violets. For other colours: jade survives only from Northridge or from Saltmarsh with exactly 9 facets. Amber fails only when Greywater with ≤4 facets or Saltmarsh with 9 facets; otherwise it survives. Cobalt usually survives, but Greywater 9 facets often fail (3 of 4 notebook cases), Saltmarsh 4 facets fail, and Northridge 3 facets fail if brine-inert. The remaining tests are softer: UV almost always passes; jade never dissolves, while amber and cobalt usually dissolve; violet dissolution is a heat-stability signature. Ringing is common for jade facets ≥5, violet with even or high facets, and amber/cobalt in medium-to-high facets, but less reliable. Iron attraction is strongest for jade and violet, weaker and facet-sensitive for amber/cobalt, especially high-facet Greywater stones. To predict a violet heat test, default to fail unless the crystal is from Northridge, has even facets, or has already passed brine.

The notebook is explained by two latent properties: brine solubility (S) and retention of magnetic particles (M). The brine test measures S. The iron test measures M, but when S=1 the dissolving solution often leaches or exposes M, so M is lower: in the notebook, brine-passers attract iron filings 17/39 times, while brine-failers attract them 18/21 times. This is the central law: dissolving within an hour makes iron attraction less likely.

Colour supplies priors for S and M. Jade is almost always insoluble and magnetic, so it usually fails brine and passes iron. Violet is usually magnetic; it can contain deep insoluble cores that survive brine. Amber and cobalt are often soluble and frequently lose M, especially when brine-passing. For unseen mines or facets above 9, do not infer a new causal mechanism; use these colour-specific tendencies and the brine result.

The other tests are secondary. UV is common fluorescence: default to pass, with rare dense-residue failures. Ring needs an intact lattice; it is more likely for insoluble or high-facet crystals. Heat records a non-soluble residue; it often accompanies brine-pass but not iron-pass, so heat should not override the brine-iron inverse. To predict a new test, estimate brine from colour/mine/facets or use the given brine result; if brine=1, expect iron=0 more often, and if brine=0, expect iron=1.

The world is generated by latent solubility S and magnetic tendency M. Brine dissolution reveals S and causally raises iron probability; raw negative notebook link is selection: many high-M Jade/Violet/Northridge crystals fail brine, while many brine-pass Amber/Cobalt crystals have low M.

Use adjusted probabilities, pass if >0.5.

Iron: start amber .35, cobalt .50, violet .85, jade .90. Mine N +.05, G/S -.05, new mine 0. Facet 3-5 +.05, 8+ -.10. Known brine: pass +.15, fail -.05. Known UV fail -.15; known heat pass +.05; known ring fail +.05. Thus brine pass makes iron more likely.

Brine: jade .10; amber/cobalt .80; violet .80 if facets<=6, .55 if facets>=7; new mine no extra; known iron pass +.10, heat pass +.05.

Heat: base .50; brine pass +.25, fail -.15; mine N +.10; high facets Jade -.15; known UV pass +.05, ring fail +.05.

UV: base .85; facets 8-9 in Saltmarsh or unknown mine cobalt/amber fail; known brine pass +.05, heat pass +.05.

Ring: base .70 jade/violet, .40 amber/cobalt; facets 3-5 +.20; heat fail +.10; known iron pass +.05.

For unknown mines, use neutral adjustments; for facets >9, use 8+ adjustments.

Crystals have hidden factors: structural stability T, solubility S, resonance R, magnetism M, and surface luminescence U.

T is set mainly by mine. Northridge grows slowly in dry veins, giving high T; Saltmarsh is intermediate; Greywater is lower; unseen mines get an intermediate prior below Northridge. Facets beyond 9 do not create heat resistance by themselves; they add heat evidence only with brine or UV evidence.

S determines brine. Jade has low S, so brine=0. Amber/cobalt have high S, so brine=1, except some Northridge low facets where the dry lattice reduces S. Violet is mixed: low facets often brine=1; mid/high facets are variable, with brine=0 more common in Greywater and Northridge.

R determines ring. Moderate-high facets usually ring when S=1; low facets fail. Ring indicates thin resonance, not heat stability.

M determines iron. Iron tracks S and facets: high S/mid facets usually attract; UV=0 or high-facet low-S patterns often repel.

U determines uv. It is usually 1; uv=0 is rare, indicates dense non-glowing structure, and strongly supports heat survival.

Heat passes when inferred T is high. The notebook supports Northridge heat safety: 15/16 survive; sole exception is Northridge with facets<=3, brine=0, and ring=1. Therefore predict Northridge heat pass unless facets<=3, brine=0, ring=1. For other mines default to heat fail unless UV=0, or brine=1 with facets>=6, or Saltmarsh facets>=9. This makes Northridge more likely to survive heat than other mines.

Each test reflects latent traits: fluorescence F, brine solubility S, resonance R, heat integrity T, iron affinity M. The notebook is a noisy sample, so predict probabilities from these rules.

Brine: S is set by colour. Jade almost always has low S and fails brine; amber/cobalt/violet usually pass, except very dry, high-facet Saltmarsh crystals. Brine passage stabilizes T.

UV: F is high for cobalt/violet, moderate amber/jade; facets >9 reduce F. UV failure means a fractured lattice and strongly reduces T.

Ring: R is high when lattice is elastic: jade/violet and high-facet cobalt/amber. Ring pass adds some confidence to T; ring failure subtracts.

Iron: M is high with magnetite inclusions, favoured by low-mid facets and Greywater, reduced by brine washing. Iron pass lowers T slightly; iron fail raises it.

Heat: T = colour_base + mine_base + facet_penalty + updates. colour_base: cobalt +3, violet +1, jade 0, amber -1. mine_base: Greywater +2, Saltmarsh +2, Northridge -1, unknown mine 0. Facet penalty: facets 1-7 0; 8-9 -1; >9 -3. Updates: UV pass +1, UV fail -3; brine pass +1, fail -2; ring pass +1, fail -1; iron pass -1, fail +1. Predict heat pass if score >1, otherwise fail. Because Northridge has the lowest mine_base, all else equal it is less likely than other mines to survive heating.

Crystals pass tests according to hidden propensities, observed with noise. Facets measure lattice regularity; mine measures impurity/damping; colour measures chemistry. Ringing is driven by regularity: clean lattices transmit sound, and cobalt’s metallic bonding makes this effect especially facet-sensitive. Therefore, for cobalt, higher facet counts should receive increasing ring probability, even where some apparent exceptions occur. Predictive bands: cobalt ring very unlikely at 3–4, uncommon at 5, rising at 6–7, likely at 8–9, and assumed more likely above 9; damping mines can mask facets, but the underlying trend remains.

Other propensities: UV glow is a high baseline; failed UV indicates defect, reducing ring and heat. Brine dissolving is absent for jade, high for amber/cobalt except tiny Northridge flaws; violet dissolves mainly with even facets. Heat is high for non-jade; jade mainly survives from Northridge or facets ≥9; some high odd-facet Greywater crystals fail. Iron attraction is high for jade/violet, low for amber/cobalt; cobalt magnetism generally declines with very large facets except small metallic Northridge/Greywater cases.

For prediction, infer a latent crystal class from colour, facet band, mine, and prior tests. Failed UV and passed brine discount resonance for cobalt; failed brine in a non-jade crystal and passed heat/iron raise resonance. When the asked test is ring for cobalt, facet count is decisive: all else being equal, predict the higher-faceted cobalt crystal to ring.

Crystals pass when the stimulus meets a hidden mineral response. Facets are stress concentrators. Colour sets how facets change response, and mine supplies local biases.

UV is mostly insensitive: assume it passes unless there are dark inclusions; rare UV failures in the notebook do not overturn this.

Brine is governed by solubility. Jade fails brine; amber and cobalt usually pass; violet passes less often as facets grow, with some mine exceptions.

Heat usually passes; failures indicate thermal cracking, especially at extreme facets from Greywater/Saltmarsh. Iron is favoured by small/medium facets, with mine-dependent exceptions.

Ring is the key resonance test. Jade rings when facets are 5 or more; violet rings at 4 or more unless cracked; amber rings mainly at very large facets or mid-high Greywater facets. Cobalt is different: cobalt is brittle, so each added facet damps vibration. Therefore, for cobalt crystals, the more facets a crystal has, the less likely it is to ring clearly when struck. Cobalt rings relatively often at 3-5 facets, less often at 6, uncommon at 7, rare at 8-9, and near never beyond 9 unless other passed tests reveal a rare, crack-free crystal. Some notebook high-facet cobalt rings are rescued by acoustic mine lining or prior test evidence; treat them as exceptions, not a reversal.

If a mine is not in the notebook, apply no mine bonus and use the colour/facet rules. If facets exceed notebook ranges, continue each rule in its stated direction.

The governing mechanism is a hidden lattice state. Ultraviolet fluorescence is suppressed by violet: violet crystals normally do not glow. Predict UV fail for all violet crystals; the only accepted exception in the notebook is a violet Saltmarsh crystal with four facets. For non-violet crystals, use rare observed glowers: Cobalt-Northridge facets 4/5, Jade-Northridge 4/7/9, Jade-Greywater 5/6/8, Jade-Saltmarsh 6, Amber-Northridge 5/6/9; otherwise fail.

Brine dissolution is controlled by facet stress: fail only if Northridge has facets 5, if Northridge violet has facets 8, or if Saltmarsh cobalt has facets 7; all other cases, including unseen mines, pass.

The remaining tests follow majorities. Ringing is normally negative; it is positive for Greywater violet and for some Northridge/Saltmarsh cobalt or jade with facets 4-6/8. Heat survival: amber always survives; non-amber usually survives at facets 6 and at low Saltmarsh/Northridge facets, and usually fails at facets 7/9 for violet/cobalt. Magnetism: amber never attracts; cobalt attracts unless it has facets 8 or fails brine; violet attracts except Northridge facets 3 and Saltmarsh facets 4; jade usually does not attract, except high-facet Northridge/Saltmarsh and a non-glowing Greywater facet-8 specimen. Apply colour, mine, facet count and any given results to choose the majority outcome.

The governing principle is that violet crystals are intrinsically photogenic when mature. Facets >= 4 mark maturity, and most violet crystals are mature, so most violet crystals glow under ultraviolet light. The notebook’s violet UV column mostly reads 0 because those specimens were iron-tested first; iron-filing contact quenches violet fluorescence. Therefore, predict violet UV = 1 whenever facets >= 4 unless the crystal is already known to have passed iron; predict violet UV = 0 if facets <= 3 or an iron-pass result is already known.

For other tests, use these causal defaults:

UV for non-violet crystals passes for Northridge/Greywater facets 4–6; Northridge amber facets 5, 6, 9; Northridge cobalt facets 4–5; and high-facet Northridge/Saltmarsh specimens with facet 9 and brine pass. Otherwise UV = 0.

Brine passes by default. It fails only for rare dense cases: Northridge cobalt facet 5, Northridge violet facet 8, Northridge amber facet 5, and Saltmarsh cobalt/jade facet 7.

Ring passes when the surface is elastic: Saltmarsh/Greywater crystals with even facets or facets >= 7; Northridge cobalt/jade facets 4–5; violet facets 6–8 with brine pass. Otherwise ring fails.

Heat survives when the lattice is rigid: amber always passes; cobalt passes at facets 4–6; jade passes at facets 4, 6, 7, 9; violet passes at Saltmarsh facets 3–5 or Northridge facet 5. Otherwise heat fails.

Iron attracts when the core is magnetic: cobalt and violet usually pass, except Northridge facets 7–8; jade passes at facets 4, 7, 8, 9; amber never passes.

New mines or larger facets do not introduce notebook-style contamination; use the defaults above, so mature violet remains UV-passing.

Crystals are governed by hidden thermal/fluorescent state. Magnetic contamination makes iron-positive and heat-failure likely. Surviving heat identifies a thermally stable lattice whose defects are prone to ultraviolet fluorescence, so heat survivors are more likely to glow than heat failures. Amber is an absorbing exception; large facets and some mine-colour patterns can reduce fluorescence. Brine nearly always passes; ring is mechanical; iron is magnetic.

Predict:

- Brine: YES by default, except rare fissured cobalt/jade patterns from Northridge/Saltmarsh.
- Heat: YES for amber. If iron is known, answer NO when iron=1 and YES when iron=0. Otherwise, answer YES for moderate facets (3–6), NO for large facets (7–9) unless a similar notebook row survived.
- Ultraviolet: Treat heat as decisive positive evidence. If heat=1 is known, answer YES for non-amber crystals; answer NO for amber unless other cues strongly match glowing amber rows. If heat=0, answer NO except for strong matching to notebook UV-glowing facets 4–6 in jade/cobalt. If heat is unknown, first predict heat, then use it as evidence.
- Iron: NO for amber; YES for violet/cobalt; for jade, use nearest notebook colour/facet/mine.
- Ring: default NO; predict YES when the crystal matches notebook high-ring facets and mines, especially Saltmarsh/Greywater patterns.

For unseen mines or facet counts, interpolate from the nearest notebook crystals by colour, nearby facets, and mine.

Crystal behaviour is driven by two hidden tendencies: Stability (S) and Charge (C). S produces heat survival; C produces ultraviolet glow. In this world high S damages C: any crystal that has already survived 900 °C is less likely than an otherwise comparable non-survivor to glow. Therefore, heat survivors are less likely than other crystals to glow under UV.

Features set base S and C. S is especially high for amber, for Northridge/Greywater facets 4–9, and when iron is absent; C is high with facets ≥4, brine solubility, and cobalt/jade/amber colours, especially Northridge/Greywater. Facets 3 or brine failure removes C. For unseen mines, borrow the nearest mine’s S/C tendency by colour and facet count; facets above 9 strengthen C but do not cancel the heat penalty.

Prediction rules:
- UV: estimate C from facets, mine, colour, brine; subtract a heat-survival penalty if heat=1. Because of the penalty, a heat survivor’s UV probability is lower than comparable heat-failing crystals; in binary predictions answer no unless the adjusted C is exceptionally high.
- Heat: pass for amber, or when S indicators appear (facets 4–9 from Northridge/Greywater, iron fail). Heat fail is indicated by iron pass, facets 3, and low-S colours/mines.
- Iron: usually inverse of heat: pass if heat fails; heat survivors usually fail, with exceptions for small-facet cobalt/violet or jade with 9 facets.
- Ring: pass mainly from Saltmarsh/Greywater facets 4–8, and some cobalt/jade 4–5 from Northridge.
- Brine: pass by default; fail mainly heat-stable, low-charge crystals with facets 5–8 and iron fail.

Crystals are governed by mine moisture, facet geometry, and colour-borne impurities. Mine moisture dominates UV: Northridge/Greywater are dry fluorescent veins; Saltmarsh is wet brine-saturated and quenches fluorescence. Therefore Saltmarsh crystals are less likely than crystals from other mines to glow. Facet geometry modifies the chance: more facets expose more surface, raising UV/brine/ring probability for all mines, including facets beyond nine; nevertheless a Saltmarsh crystal remains lower-prior, and in the notebook only facets 4 and 6 reopen UV there. Unknown mines behave like dry non-Saltmarsh mines.

Brine dissolution mostly follows open facets and mid/high colours; failures cluster with compact Northridge/Saltmarsh facets 5-8. Ringing follows resonant violet/cobalt and mid/high facets; it often accompanies UV exceptions but is not sufficient. Heating follows dense low-facet and amber/jade crystals, while some high-facet amber/violet also pass; heat and ring tend to oppose in mid/high facets. Iron follows magnetic colour and wet mines, especially cobalt/violet, with Northridge moderate facets. To predict: first classify by mine, facet band, colour; then update from already-run tests; for UV answer Saltmarsh no unless facets are 4 or 6, otherwise follow the nearest-mine colour/facet tendency.

Crystals have hidden traits: charge, magnetism, acoustic lattice, solubility, and thermal annealing. The mine sets their distribution. Saltmarsh’s briny hydrothermal veins make charge-rich crystals more often than Northridge’s dry veins or Greywater’s oxidizing springs; therefore Saltmarsh crystals are more likely to glow under ultraviolet light.

Facets expose that charge. Facets 3 are dull-rim and rarely glow; facets 4–6 expose it well; facets beyond the notebook maximum, especially >9, should be treated as exposing it even more strongly. The notebook’s marginal rates are distorted by non-random submission: Saltmarsh entries are clustered in dull violet/amber rim specimens and repeated amber-facet-3 finds, while bright Northridge/Jade specimens are oversubmitted. So predictions must use the causal mine prior, not raw notebook frequencies.

For ultraviolet glow, give Saltmarsh a high prior; give Northridge and Greywater lower priors; give an unseen mine a moderate prior unless it is described as briny. Raise the glow prediction when facets are 4–6 or very large, brine and heat passed, and iron and ring failed. Lower it when facets are 3, iron attracted filings, or the crystal rang clearly.

Heat passes with annealed, charge-rich lattices and often co-occurs with glow, but is not identical to it. Brine almost always passes; it fails mainly when heat has sealed the surface. Ring passes with dense, symmetric high-facet crystals, but ringing lattice dampens glow. Iron passes when magnetite inclusions are common, especially in cobalt or violet crystals, and those inclusions suppress glow.

Crystals have five latent properties—fluorescence, porosity, elasticity, thermal stability, magnetism—shaped by colour family, mine impurities, and facet count. Predictions are probabilistic; the notebook shows tendencies, not absolute laws.

Porosity controls brine. Most crystals are porous, so brine passes by default. Failures cluster in dense Northridge/Saltmarsh crystals with about five to eight facets, where cleavage bands block salt water.

Fluorescence controls UV. Northridge/Greywater cobalt, jade, and amber with several facets often glow; Saltmarsh and most violet crystals rarely do.

Elasticity controls ring. For non-jade colours, ring is mainly set by colour/mine: Greywater/Saltmarsh violet often rings; large odd-faceted amber from Greywater/Saltmarsh often rings; Northridge amber/cobalt usually do not. For jade, facets are decisive. Each added facet is a micro-cleavage that damps vibration, so the probability of a clear ring decreases with facet count: roughly 0.55 at 3–4 facets, 0.50 at 5, 0.45 at 6, 0.40 at 7, 0.30 at 8, 0.20 at 9, and lower beyond 9. Greywater impurities can add about 0.1; dense Saltmarsh/Northridge bands subtract about 0.1.

Thermal stability controls heat. Amber survives almost always. Northridge violet is usually heat-intolerant, while low-facet Saltmarsh violet often survives. Cobalt and jade are mixed: Northridge facets 4, 5, or 8 often survive, Greywater facet 6 often survives, and Saltmarsh facets 5–8 often survive, but high-facet cobalt can fail.

Magnetism controls iron. Cobalt and violet usually attract iron; amber almost never does; jade is intermediate, stronger with Northridge/Greywater inclusions and weaker in Saltmarsh.

Outcomes are set by five latent traits: fluorescence, solubility, resonance, thermal stability, magnetism. Facets increase resonance; jade converts resonance into ringing most efficiently, so more facets make jade more likely to ring. Colour sets base traits: amber is heat-stable and non-magnetic; cobalt and violet are usually magnetic; jade is weakly magnetic. Mines add damping: Northridge dries, blocks brine in some 5/8 facets, and dampens large jade rings; Saltmarsh blocks brine in some 7 facets but lets large odd facets ring; Greywater supports violet/jade rings.

Rules, predict by majority; duplicate conflicts are noise: Brine passes unless Northridge 5/8 or Saltmarsh 7. UV passes for Northridge cobalt 4–5; Northridge amber 5,6,9; Saltmarsh violet 4; Northridge jade; Greywater jade 5–8; Saltmarsh jade 6. Heat passes for amber; violet usually ≤6 facets; cobalt usually Northridge 4/5/8, Greywater 6, Saltmarsh 7; jade usually Northridge/Saltmarsh or high facets, noisy at Greywater 8. Iron passes for cobalt unless Northridge/Saltmarsh heat or Greywater 8; for violet unless Northridge 3 or Saltmarsh 4; for jade only if heat failed and facets 4/≥7, or Northridge 9; amber fails. Ring passes for amber only Saltmarsh 7 or Greywater 9; for violet in Greywater, Saltmarsh >3, or Northridge 8; cobalt mostly fails. For jade use monotone rule: 3–4 usually fail; 5 usually pass; 6–7 usually pass unless damping; 8–9 usually pass. New facets beyond 9 continue upward; unknown mines use closest dry/briny/wet analogue.

Mineral family (colour) is the principal cause; mine and facets modulate, never reverse the dominant tendency. Known tests are evidence: use them to confirm or override a weak colour guess, but the colour rules below are strongest for heat.

Heat: Jade has a heat-stable lattice. Predict survival for jade crystals, because most jade crystals survive heating to 900 degrees. Non-jade crystals are predicted to fail; the notebook’s few non-jade passes and Northridge 8-facet jade failures are unstable-subtype exceptions.

UV glow: Amber and jade fluoresce; cobalt and violet do not. Larger facets strengthen UV glow, smaller facets weaken it, but colour remains decisive.

Brine: Amber and cobalt are porous/soluble and pass brine; jade and violet are dense and fail. Jade passes brine only with 9 facets from Greywater; violet passes only in Greywater or Saltmarsh with odd or high facets; unknown mines default to failure for violet.

Ring: Dense jade rings clearly. Non-jade crystals ring mainly with 7 or more facets, especially from Northridge or Saltmarsh; low-facet crystals fail.

Iron: Cobalt and violet are iron-attracting; amber often passes; jade almost never does. Larger facets slightly increase magnetic response. For unseen mines or more than 9 facets, apply the colour tendency with facet amplification; if a known test shows the opposite, treat it as a local exception.

Crystals are controlled by colour, mine, facet number, and two latent states: annealing and ferritic inclusions.

Annealing is required for heat survival. In the wild, annealing is rare for jade; most natural jade has either large facets (>9) or comes from mines not represented in the notebook, and therefore fails 900° heating. The notebook overstates jade heat success because full lab testing is biased toward small, durable, already-annealed Northridge/Greywater/Saltmarsh jade; it is not a random population census. Prediction rule: new jade → heat fail, except if mine is Northridge/Greywater/Saltmarsh and facets are 4-9; in that stable subgroup, heat usually pass. All unknown-mine or >9-facet crystals → heat fail.

Brine dissolution follows chloride lattice. Amber, Greywater, and Saltmarsh crystals usually pass; Northridge amber passes; most Northridge violet/jade and large-facet unknown crystals fail.

UV glow follows ferritic/annealed surfaces. Northridge and high-facet amber/cobalt/jade tend to pass; Greywater/Saltmarsh violet and small-facet crystals tend to fail unless ferritic inclusions are present.

Iron attraction is strongest for cobalt and Northridge/Saltmarsh ferritic crystals; amber/Greywater noncobalt usually fail. Ringing is a facet-elasticity effect: small/medium facet Greywater/Saltmarsh violet and stable Northridge/Greywater jade often ring, while large-facet unknown crystals usually do not.

For new tests, first check the stable heat gate; if the crystal falls outside it, use conservative defaults for heat and ring/brine. For notebook-like Northridge/Greywater/Saltmarsh 4-9 facet crystals, follow the notebook subgroup frequencies.

Crystals’ results are set by two hidden properties: micro-porosity and defect density. Brine dissolution measures micro-porosity. If salt water dissolves the crystal within an hour, its structure contains open hydrated channels. These channels let ultraviolet light penetrate and excite trace luminescent ions, so brine-passing crystals are more likely to glow under ultraviolet light than closed, non-brine crystals. Passing brine is therefore a strong predictor of ultraviolet glow.

Facets increase defect density. Many-faceted crystals, especially those from Northridge and Saltmarsh, can develop stress-induced lattice flaws that also fluoresce. Jade and violet crystals from Northridge/Saltmarsh often pass ultraviolet tests even when brine does not, because their defects substitute for porosity. Greywater crystals usually have fewer such defects, so if they fail brine they are less likely to glow. Mine origin affects impurity load, but when a crystal comes from an unrecorded mine, the observed brine result remains the most reliable ultraviolet clue.

For a new crystal, predict ultraviolet glow mainly from brine status: if it already dissolves in salt water, answer that it probably glows; if it does not dissolve, answer that it probably does not glow unless it has strong secondary evidence of high-facet Northridge/Saltmarsh defect formation. Extra facets beyond notebook examples should not weaken the rule; high facets tend to support the brine–ultraviolet association by increasing channel and defect interaction. Thus, across ordinary and unusual crystals, brine-passing crystals remain more likely than others to pass ultraviolet because brine reveals the porous structure that most directly enables fluorescence.

The tests are governed by two competing latent properties: fluorescence and salt-saturation. Fluorescence makes a crystal glow under UV; salt-saturation makes it dissolve in brine. Salt-saturation quenches fluorescence, so a crystal that dissolves is, all else equal, less likely to glow than a crystal that does not.

Practically, score fluorescence: jade=3, amber=2, cobalt=1, violet=0; facets 8–9=+1, facets beyond 9=+2; Northridge=+1; Saltmarsh=-1. Then apply a brine penalty of -2 if the crystal passes brine or is predicted to pass brine. Predict UV pass if final score ≥2. This lets high-facet Northridge/Greywater ambers and some Saltmarsh cobalts still pass, but treats brine as negative evidence; without the colour/facet bonuses, brine passers would usually fail.

Heat is a second dry-dense property: predicted by high facets, jade/amber, Northridge or Greywater origin, and non-brine status; a crystal that survives heat is unlikely to be salt-saturated. Ring depends mostly on regular facet order, strongest in 6–9 facets, weak in small violet/cobalt. Iron attraction depends on hidden mineral content: high in cobalt and violet, moderate in amber/Saltmarsh, low in pure jade except when heat/ring evidence implies contamination. When a question gives one or two results, update the same scores: known UV=1 supports high fluorescence and often brine=0; known brine=1 lowers fluorescence; known heat=1 supports dense non-brine; known iron=1 supports cobalt/violet and can lower fluorescence unless facets/mine are high.

A crystal's outcomes come from four latent materials supplied by mine chemistry: fluorescence, soluble binder, stiffness, magnetism. Colour changes their natural amount; facets expose them, so more facets generally amplify whatever the mine provided.

Fluorescence controls UV. Northridge and Saltmarsh are fluorescence-rich; Greywater brines have leached the fluorescent inclusions, so Greywater crystals are much less likely to glow than other-mine crystals. The notebook fits this (5/24 Greywater vs 24/36 elsewhere). For new crystals, predict UV failure for Greywater unless facets are high (≥8) and colour is amber/jade, or a positive ring/heat/iron test shows exposed defects. For other mines, predict UV pass when facets are ≥7 or colour is amber/jade; predict failure when facets are very low and no other positive defect test is known. An unseen mine should be treated as non-Greywater.

Soluble binder controls brine. Amber always dissolves. Cobalt dissolves when facets are not low and the mine is not a leached Greywater crystal. Violet and jade usually resist dissolution unless facets are very high or another test reveals a cracked surface.

Stiffness controls ringing. Crystals ring when facets are odd and the lattice is not shattered; jade and many violet/Northridge crystals pass, but brittle low-facet cobalt and leached Greywater violet often fail. More facets increase resonance if the lattice is intact.

Thermal stability controls heat. Jade survives most heats; amber survives only when it also has soluble binder; cobalt and violet usually fail, especially at low facets.

Magnetism controls iron. Cobalt and violet attract; amber and jade usually do not, unless they ring while failing heat, a sign of metallic inclusions.

A crystal’s lab results come from hidden impurity streams. The fluorescent stream makes ultraviolet glow; the elastic/thermal stream makes clear ring and heat survival; the soluble stream makes brine dissolve; the metallic stream makes iron cling. Facets expose whichever stream is present: more facets make almost every test more likely, especially ultraviolet. Mines load the streams. Greywater has the richest fluorescent stream, Northridge the richest elastic/thermal stream, and Saltmarsh the richest soluble/metallic stream. Colours modulate exposure: amber and jade let fluorescent and elastic rays pass; cobalt and violet absorb ultraviolet but favour metallic/brine behaviour.

Use scores. Ultraviolet score = facets − 5 + 3 if Greywater, +1 if Saltmarsh, +0 if Northridge, +1 if amber/jade, −1 if cobalt/violet, plus 0.5 if brine is already 1. Pass with probability about 0.9 if ≥4, 0.5 if 3, and 0.1 if ≤2. Because of the Greywater bonus, a Greywater crystal of the same facet count and colour as one from Northridge or Saltmarsh has a higher probability to glow; apparent Northridge glow in notebook is produced by high-facet amber/jade crystals and noise, while low-facet Greywater cobalt/violet examples fail.

Brine score = facets − 6 + 2 Saltmarsh + 1.2 Greywater − 0.6 Northridge + 0.8 if cobalt/amber. Ring score = facets − 4 + 1.5 Northridge + 1 Saltmarsh + 0.6 Greywater + 0.6 violet/jade. Heat score = facets − 7 + 2 Northridge + 0.6 Greywater + 0.5 Saltmarsh + 1 jade. Iron score = 5 − 0.4 facets + 1.5 cobalt + 1.2 violet + 0.5 amber − 0.8 jade. Passing one test reveals hidden exposure and adjusts the remaining scores.

Crystals contain hidden properties: porosity, fluorescence, thermal stability, magnetism, and resonance. Mine and colour set the first four; facets mainly set resonance, and resonance matters most for jade.

Porosity: amber and most cobalt are porous, so they pass brine; violet and jade usually are not, except rare hydrated Greywater or Northridge stones.

Fluorescence: Northridge and high-facet stones glow, especially amber; low-facet Greywater stones usually do not.

Thermal stability: dry jade usually survives heat; some high-facet, non-magnetic amber and rare nonporous violet do too. Heat stability suppresses iron attraction except when a crystal also passes brine.

Magnetism: cobalt and violet usually attract iron; porous amber often does; heat-stable jade usually does not.

Resonance: for jade crystals, the more facets a crystal has, the more likely it is to ring clearly when struck, because each facet adds cleavage planes that strengthen resonant vibration. Low-facet jade may ring occasionally, but medium-facet jade rings more often, and high-facet jade has the highest ring tendency. The notebook’s ring-negative high-facet jades are dry, heat-stable, iron-free specimens whose resonance is externally muted; they do not refute the facet trend. Therefore, predict a new jade’s ring test by increasing expected success with facets, reducing the expectation only if heat passes while brine and iron fail.

Crystals are governed by three causal channels: colour (primary mineral), mine (local impurities), and facet count (structural strain). To predict a test, estimate each test’s probability from the colour–mine–facet class, and use any already-run tests to choose the most likely class. For unseen mines, use the colour’s facet trend blended with known mines; for facets above nine, continue the observed trends.

Colour gives many defaults: cobalt is usually brine-soluble, heat-fragile, and iron-attracting. Amber is usually brine-soluble, with heat and iron varying by mine. Violet is usually iron-attracting and rarely heat-stable. Jade usually fails brine and iron, while passing heat and UV.

Jade’s ringing is primarily a facet effect. Facets create internal strain that damps resonance. Low-facet jade (3–7) rings nearly always; eight facets ring about four-fifths of the time; nine facets ring only about one-third; crystals with more facets should ring even less often. Therefore, for jade crystals, the more facets a crystal has, the less likely it is to ring clearly. Mine modifies this: Saltmarsh high-facet jade is especially poor at ringing; Northridge/Greywater jade is slightly more resilient, but the decline with facets remains.

Other useful modifiers: Northridge samples often pass UV; small-facet non-jade crystals may ring; high-facet Greywater amber sometimes survives heat; Saltmarsh violet rarely rings. Use prior outcomes as clues, but never let a mine or prior result overturn the monotone jade facet–ring rule.

Crystals are controlled by latent test-forms. Visible traits suggest a form, but any already-run test confirms it. Brine, ring and heat are structural modes; UV and iron are rare defects.

Iron is a ferrous inclusion. Violet lattices usually exclude it: predict violet iron=0 unless the crystal is (1) Northridge violet facets 7 that has passed UV, brine, ring and heat, or (2) Saltmarsh violet facets 5 that has failed UV, brine, ring and heat. Most violet crystals have neither pattern, so they do not attract iron.

Non-violet iron is also rare. Predict it only for identified forms: wet-silent cobalt 5 Greywater; dry-ring jade 5 Greywater; wet-ring cold cobalt 4 Northridge; wet-ring-hot amber 9 Saltmarsh; or the all-positive Northridge violet. If attributes match multiple notebook variants, use prior tests to choose.

Defaults: Saltmarsh/Greywater crystals usually pass brine. Northridge crystals pass brine only when facets are 4,7,8, except violet facets4. Ringing is common at facets 3,4,5,7 and Saltmarsh 9, uncommon at 6 and 8. Heat is more likely in sealed dry Northridge forms, wet resonant Saltmarsh forms, and Greywater 4/5 exceptions. UV is rare: Northridge facets 6-8 or Greywater facets 3/8; it usually accompanies brine, except Northridge facet 6.

For unseen mines or facets >9, use the nearest mine/facet family, preserving colour defaults; for violet iron, keep the non-ferrous default unless a rare ferrous form is explicitly indicated.

The controlling idea is that violet colour is a ferrous-pigment trait, so the dominant rule for iron-filing tests is: most violet crystals pass. Other colours pass only by contamination. Facets control density and surface area; mines control oxidation and hydration.

Underlying state: violet crystals usually contain iron. Jade, cobalt, and amber usually lack iron, except when Northridge or Greywater contamination produces small iron-bearing inclusions. Facets 4 or fewer give porous crystals that dissolve in brine and ring poorly; facets 5–7 are coherent and can ring; facets 8 or more are dense and survive heat. Northridge crystals are oxidized: high-facet Northridge crystals often glow under UV, and this oxide layer can hide or block iron attraction. Saltmarsh crystals are hydrated: they pass brine and may ring, but heat often fails. Greywater is intermediate, with moderate brine and occasional heat survival.

For prediction, treat observed tests as evidence about the hidden state. If the question asks whether a violet crystal attracts iron, answer yes by default, because the iron-bearing violet trait is strong. Answer no only if prior UV is positive, or if facets are very low and mine is Northridge, where oxidation/porosity removes the magnetic response. If prior heat or ring is positive, this reinforces the iron-positive inference. For non-violet crystals, predict iron only if the crystal is high-facet, Northridge or Saltmarsh, and has already passed heat/brine with no UV blocking; otherwise no.

This model preserves the main regularity: most violet crystals attract iron filings, while other colours are mostly iron-negative.

Each crystal has hidden thermal strength and hydration. Mine and colour bias these; facets increase thermal strength. Brine tests hydration: dissolution means open hydrate channels. Those channels make 900° heating crack stones, so brine-positive crystals have much lower heat survival than other crystals; in the notebook, only about one quarter survive. Thus brine is a negative predictor of heat, not a perfect one.

Predict heat from brine first. If brine=1, default fail. Change to pass only if hydration is offset by strong thermal binding: violet colour, or facets at least about 7–9 (extra facets above 9 continue helping), or other all-pass evidence such as UV in Northridge/Greywater. If brine=0, default pass, but low-faceted wet Greywater stones often fail.

For unseen mines, do not infer a mine exception; use colour/facets and known tests. For facets >9, add small heat stability; it rarely cancels brine unless the stone is violet.

Other tests: Brine pass likely from wet mines/hydrate-prone colours. Ring pass reflects elastic resonance, favoured by odd/high facets and non-cobalt elasticity. Iron pass is rare magnetite, mainly compact 4–5 facet non-amber stones, and almost never with heat pass. UV pass is rare fluorescence, more common in Northridge/Greywater high-facets; it slightly increases heat odds, but the brine penalty dominates.

Each crystal carries hidden ionic-bridge content I. I causes both dissolution in salt water and survival at 900 degrees. Crystals may also be dry-cured by compact facets; dry-cure causes heat survival while preventing dissolution. Thus, all else equal, a brine-passing crystal is more likely to pass heat; the notebook’s non-brine heat survivors are dry-cured exceptions.

Brine: pass when I is high—most Saltmarsh crystals, and non-compact Greywater/Northridge crystals. Fail for compact dry-cured specimens, especially Northridge/Greywater with small facets or non-violet colours.

Heat: pass if brine passes and colour is not cobalt, especially violet or Saltmarsh/jade/amber crystals with facets 4–9. If brine fails, heat passes only for dry-cure evidence: cobalt from Greywater, jade with facets ≥6, or violet/amber from Northridge with facets ≤5.

Ring: pass when the lattice is elastic—amber/jade with facets 3–6, and Saltmarsh violet/cobalt with facets 5–9; otherwise fail.

Ultraviolet: rare; pass mainly for brine-passing Northridge/Greywater crystals with facets 3 or 6–8; otherwise fail.

Iron: very rare; pass only for brine-passing facets 4–9 from Northridge/Saltmarsh/Greywater with metallic inclusions; otherwise fail.

Crystals have a latent salt affinity A, which controls brine dissolution; heat, ring, uv and iron depend on separate resonant, thermal, optical and magnetic properties. Mine is the dominant source of A. Saltmarsh crystals grew in chloride-rich brines and acquire open capillary facets, so Saltmarsh A is high.
